subtopic_detail: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes at thirty weeks with no clinical infection and a cephalic presentation
stem:
A 29 year old woman at 30 weeks in her second pregnancy presents to your birth suite after a sudden gush of clear fluid four hours ago, with continued leaking since. She has no abdominal pain and reports normal foetal movements.

Sterile speculum examination shows a pool of clear liquor in the posterior fornix with a closed cervix and no offensive odour. Her uterus is soft and non-tender on palpation, and the presentation is cephalic on ultrasound with an amniotic fluid index at the lower limit of normal. Cardiotocography shows a baseline of 140/min with normal variability, accelerations present and no decelerations. Her observations and blood results are reassuring.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82/min, blood pressure 114/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C, foetal heart rate baseline 140/min
data_table.Examination: Pool of clear liquor in the posterior fornix, closed cervix, no offensive odour, soft non-tender uterus
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 9.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 4 mg/L (<5), low vaginal swab sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin with clavulanate and corticosteroids with inpatient expectant surveillance
options.rationale: This combination is specifically avoided in this setting because it is associated with an increased rate of neonatal necrotising enterocolitis. The principle of latency antibiotics is right but the agent is wrong. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.text: Oral erythromycin with antenatal corticosteroids and inpatient expectant surveillance
options.rationale: Latency antibiotics prolong pregnancy and reduce neonatal morbidity, and corticosteroids reduce respiratory distress, intraventricular haemorrhage and necrotising enterocolitis at this gestation. With no evidence of infection or foetal compromise, expectant management allows further maturation. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.text: Antenatal corticosteroids with tocolysis for 48 hours and inpatient expectant surveillance
options.rationale: Tocolysis is not recommended once membranes have ruptured because it does not improve outcomes and may prolong exposure to intrauterine infection. She is not contracting in any case. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.text: Antenatal corticosteroids with induction of labour once the second dose has been given
options.rationale: Immediate birth at 30 weeks exchanges a small infection risk for substantial prematurity, and expectant management is preferred while surveillance remains reassuring. Planned birth becomes appropriate closer to 37 weeks. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.text: Antenatal corticosteroids with amnioinfusion and inpatient expectant surveillance
options.rationale: Amnioinfusion has no established role in managing ruptured membranes remote from term and introduces an additional intrauterine procedure. The fluid volume here is in any case at the lower limit of normal. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

explanation.summary: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes is confirmed on sterile speculum examination rather than by digital examination, which should be avoided because it introduces infection and shortens latency. Management balances the risk of ascending infection against the risks of prematurity, and while both surveillance and the threshold for birth shift with gestation, expectant management is preferred well before term. Latency antibiotics are given to prolong the interval to birth, with a macrolide chosen because co-amoxiclav increases neonatal necrotising enterocolitis. Antenatal corticosteroids are given for foetal lung maturity, and magnesium sulfate is added for neuroprotection when birth is anticipated before 30 weeks. Signs of chorioamnionitis, including maternal fever, uterine tenderness, offensive liquor, maternal tachycardia or foetal tachycardia, convert the plan to immediate birth with intravenous antibiotics.
key_points: Diagnosis is by sterile speculum examination, avoiding digital examination
Latency antibiotics use a macrolide, not amoxicillin with clavulanate
Tocolysis is not recommended after membranes rupture
Magnesium sulfate is given for neuroprotection when birth is expected before 30 weeks
Chorioamnionitis converts management from expectant to immediate birth
explanation.pearls: Amoxicillin with clavulanate is specifically avoided as the latency antibiotic in ruptured preterm membranes because of the increased rate of neonatal necrotising enterocolitis demonstrated in the ORACLE trial.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

subtopic_detail: Prevention of further seizures in a man who had a witnessed fit thirty hours after his last drink
stem:
A 52 year old man is admitted under your team after a witnessed generalised seizure at home. He drinks about 20 standard drinks daily and his last drink was thirty hours before the seizure, having stopped because he ran out of money.

He has no history of epilepsy and has never had a seizure before. He is now alert and oriented with a mild tremor of the outstretched hands and is sweating lightly. His computed tomography brain scan is normal and there is no head injury. His electrolytes, glucose and magnesium are within normal limits, and his withdrawal scale score is 12.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 106/min, blood pressure 156/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 37.1 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert and oriented, mild tremor of outstretched hands, light sweating, no focal neurological signs, no head injury
data_table.Investigations: Electrolytes glucose and magnesium within normal limits, computed tomography brain normal, withdrawal scale score 12

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment to prevent further seizures?

options.text: A loading regimen of oral phenytoin with parenteral thiamine given before any glucose
options.rationale: Antiepileptic drugs are ineffective for withdrawal seizures because the mechanism is receptor mediated central nervous system hyperexcitability rather than an epileptic focus. They are indicated when an independent seizure disorder coexists. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine)

options.text: A loading regimen of oral carbamazepine with parenteral thiamine given before any glucose
options.rationale: Carbamazepine has some role in mild withdrawal in ambulatory settings in other countries but is not the Australian approach and is not adequate after a seizure. Benzodiazepine cover is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine)

options.text: Oral haloperidol as required with parenteral thiamine given before any glucose
options.rationale: Antipsychotics lower the seizure threshold and would increase the risk of a further seizure. They are used only as an adjunct for hallucinations once benzodiazepine cover is adequate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine)

options.text: A loading regimen of oral diazepam with parenteral thiamine given before any glucose
options.rationale: Long acting benzodiazepines are the only agents shown to prevent recurrent withdrawal seizures, and diazepam self tapers through its active metabolites. Parenteral thiamine precedes glucose because a glucose load in a thiamine deplete patient can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine)

options.text: Symptom triggered oral diazepam only when his withdrawal scale score exceeds 15
options.rationale: A symptom triggered threshold approach is reasonable for uncomplicated withdrawal but is inadequate once a seizure has occurred, since the seizure marks a higher risk course. Front loading provides immediate protection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine)

explanation.summary: Alcohol withdrawal seizures typically occur between six and forty eight hours after the last drink, are generalised tonic clonic, and usually occur singly or in a short cluster without focal features. A first seizure in this context still warrants imaging and biochemical assessment, since head injury, hypoglycaemia and electrolyte disturbance are common in this population and can coexist. Benzodiazepines are the treatment of choice because they restore the inhibitory tone lost when chronic alcohol exposure is withdrawn, and conventional antiepileptic drugs do not prevent recurrence. A loading or front loaded regimen with a long acting agent gives immediate protection and a pharmacologically smooth taper, and is preferred to symptom triggered dosing once a seizure has occurred. Thiamine is given parenterally before any carbohydrate load, and having had a withdrawal seizure identifies a patient at higher risk of progressing to delirium tremens, which warrants closer observation over the following days.
key_points: Withdrawal seizures occur six to forty eight hours after the last drink
Benzodiazepines prevent recurrence and antiepileptic drugs do not
Loading with a long acting agent is preferred once a seizure has occurred
Parenteral thiamine precedes any glucose administration
A withdrawal seizure predicts higher risk of later delirium tremens
explanation.pearls: Giving intravenous glucose before thiamine to a chronically alcohol dependent patient can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy, so parenteral thiamine goes in first even when the blood glucose is low.

subtopic_detail: Muscle aching without weakness and a normal creatine kinase six weeks after starting a statin
stem:
A 58 year old man attends your practice six weeks after starting atorvastatin 40 mg daily for secondary prevention following a myocardial infarction. He reports aching in both thighs and shoulders that came on gradually over the past fortnight.

He describes it as a dull ache rather than weakness, and he can still climb stairs and rise from a chair without difficulty. His urine is a normal colour. On examination his power is 5 out of 5 in all muscle groups with no tenderness and normal reflexes. His creatine kinase, thyroid function, renal function and liver enzymes are all within normal limits. He tells you he has read that statins damage muscle and he wants to stop the drug permanently.

data_table.Examination: Power 5 out of 5 in all muscle groups, no muscle tenderness, normal reflexes, normal gait
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 142 U/L (<200), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, creatinine within normal limits, liver enzymes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease the statin permanently and manage his lipids with dietary measures and exercise alone
options.rationale: Abandoning statin therapy after a myocardial infarction removes a treatment with a clear mortality benefit on the basis of symptoms that are frequently not drug related. Lifestyle measures alone will not achieve his lipid targets. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Continue the same statin at the same dose and add coenzyme Q10 supplementation daily
options.rationale: Coenzyme Q10 has not been shown in randomised trials to relieve statin associated muscle symptoms and adds cost without benefit. Continuing unchanged also ignores his stated intention to stop. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Continue the same statin and arrange electromyography with a muscle biopsy for further assessment
options.rationale: Invasive investigation is reserved for objective weakness with a markedly raised creatine kinase, which would raise the possibility of an immune mediated necrotising myopathy. His examination and enzymes do not support that. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Cease the statin permanently and commence a proprotein convertase subtilisin kexin inhibitor now
options.rationale: These agents are reserved for patients with a documented inability to tolerate statins after adequate rechallenge, and Australian subsidy requires that demonstration. Moving to them first bypasses a necessary step. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Cease the statin for a washout period, then rechallenge at a lower dose of a different statin
options.rationale: A normal creatine kinase with preserved power excludes true myopathy, and most such symptoms are not reproduced on blinded rechallenge, so permanent avoidance forfeits substantial mortality benefit unnecessarily. A structured washout and rechallenge establishes whether the drug is genuinely responsible. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Muscle symptoms are the commonest reason patients stop statins, yet blinded rechallenge studies consistently show that the great majority of such symptoms occur equally on placebo, meaning they are often not caused by the drug. The clinically important distinction is between statin associated muscle symptoms with a normal creatine kinase and preserved power, which are common and manageable, and true myopathy or rhabdomyolysis with objective weakness and a markedly raised enzyme, which is rare and requires immediate cessation. A third entity, immune mediated necrotising myopathy, presents with proximal weakness and a very high creatine kinase that persists after stopping the drug and requires immunosuppression. The recommended approach to the common presentation is to exclude contributors such as hypothyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, renal impairment and interacting drugs, then to stop the statin for a washout, confirm symptom resolution, and rechallenge with a lower dose or an alternative agent. Alternate day dosing of a long acting statin is often tolerated when daily dosing is not.
key_points: Most statin attributed muscle symptoms are not reproduced on blinded rechallenge
Normal creatine kinase with preserved power excludes true myopathy
Immune mediated necrotising myopathy persists after the drug is stopped
Exclude hypothyroidism, vitamin D deficiency and interacting drugs first
Alternate day dosing of a long acting statin is often tolerated
explanation.pearls: A creatine kinase that stays markedly elevated weeks after the statin is stopped, with genuine proximal weakness, points to immune mediated necrotising myopathy rather than ordinary intolerance, and that patient needs immunosuppression rather than a rechallenge.

subtopic_detail: Imaging choice and timing for a newborn girl with a family history of hip problems and a stable clinical examination
stem:
You review a 3 day old girl on the postnatal ward before discharge. She was born at term in a cephalic presentation after an uncomplicated pregnancy and birth, and she is feeding and behaving normally.

Her mother mentions that her own sister was in a harness as a baby for a hip problem. On your examination the Ortolani and Barlow manoeuvres are both negative, hip abduction is full and symmetrical, and leg lengths and skin creases are equal. The rest of the newborn examination including the spine is normal. Her mother asks whether anything further needs to be arranged.

data_table.Examination: Ortolani and Barlow manoeuvres negative bilaterally, full symmetrical hip abduction, equal leg lengths and symmetrical skin creases, normal spine
data_table.Birth history: Term cephalic vaginal birth, birth weight 3.4 kg, uncomplicated pregnancy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange a hip ultrasound before discharge from the postnatal ward this week
options.rationale: Scanning in the first days of life commonly shows physiological immaturity from maternal hormones and generates false positives with unnecessary follow up. The examination timing, not the modality, is what is wrong here. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

options.text: Arrange a hip ultrasound at six weeks of age and review her with the result
options.rationale: A first degree family history is a risk factor that warrants imaging even when the examination is normal, because dysplasia can be present without instability. Scanning is deferred to about six weeks so that normal neonatal laxity has resolved and the study is interpretable. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

options.text: Arrange a pelvic radiograph at six weeks of age and review her with the result
options.rationale: The femoral head is not ossified at this age so radiography cannot assess the joint reliably, and ultrasound is the modality of choice. Radiography becomes useful once the ossific nucleus appears at around four to six months. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

options.text: Provide double nappy padding and arrange clinical review at six weeks of age
options.rationale: Double nappies are not an effective treatment or substitute for imaging and may falsely reassure the family. Clinical review alone will miss dysplasia without instability. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

options.text: Give routine discharge advice with no imaging and rely on child health checks
options.rationale: Relying on serial examination alone misses the dysplastic but stable hip, which is exactly the pattern that a family history predicts. Risk factors change the screening pathway even when examination is normal. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

explanation.summary: Developmental dysplasia of the hip is screened clinically in every newborn, but clinical examination detects instability rather than dysplasia and therefore misses a proportion of affected hips. Selective ultrasound is added for recognised risk factors, principally a first degree family history and breech presentation in later pregnancy. The timing of the scan matters as much as the decision to order it, because maternal hormone mediated laxity in the first weeks produces immature appearances that resolve spontaneously and generate false positives. A frankly dislocated or dislocatable hip on examination is a different situation and needs urgent orthopaedic referral rather than a routine scan.
key_points: Clinical examination detects instability but can miss dysplasia without instability
First degree family history and breech presentation prompt selective ultrasound
Ultrasound is deferred to around six weeks to avoid physiological false positives
Radiography is unhelpful until the femoral head ossifies at four to six months
An abnormal examination needs orthopaedic referral rather than routine imaging
explanation.pearls: A positive Ortolani or Barlow test at the newborn check bypasses the six week ultrasound pathway entirely and goes straight to orthopaedic referral, because a dislocatable hip is a treatment decision rather than a screening question.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip
Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Newborn hip screening

subtopic_detail: Antenatal surveillance and birth planning after a low anterior placenta is reported in a woman with two previous caesareans
stem:
A 34 year old woman at 21 weeks in her third pregnancy attends your antenatal clinic to discuss her morphology scan. Her two previous births were both by caesarean section, the first for breech presentation and the second as a planned repeat procedure.

She is well with no bleeding and no pain. The morphology scan reports an anterior placenta that reaches the internal os, with loss of the normal hypoechoic retroplacental clear zone and several irregular vascular lacunae within the placental substance in the region overlying the previous uterine scar. Foetal growth and anatomy are normal. She tells you she has read that a low placenta usually moves up, and asks whether she can plan to give birth at her local unit as she did last time.

data_table.Imaging: Anterior placenta reaching the internal os, loss of the retroplacental clear zone, irregular vascular lacunae overlying the previous uterine scar, normal foetal growth and anatomy
data_table.Obstetric history: Two previous caesarean sections, no antepartum bleeding in this pregnancy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan?

options.text: Refer to a tertiary centre for specialist imaging and a planned caesarean with surgical backup
options.rationale: Loss of the clear zone with lacunae in an anterior placenta overlying a previous scar indicates abnormal placental invasion rather than simple praevia. Outcomes are substantially better when birth occurs in a centre with interventional radiology, blood bank and gynaecological oncology or urology support available. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta accreta spectrum)

options.text: Repeat the transvaginal scan at 32 weeks and plan a caesarean locally if it remains low
options.rationale: This is the correct pathway for uncomplicated placenta praevia, where migration is common and local birth is reasonable. The invasion features here mean the problem is not the position of the placenta but its attachment. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia)

options.text: Reassure her that most low placentas resolve and review the position again at 36 weeks
options.rationale: Reassurance based on migration ignores the sonographic features of invasion, which do not resolve and carry a high risk of catastrophic haemorrhage. It also defers referral past the point where planning is useful. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta accreta spectrum)

options.text: Admit her from 28 weeks for inpatient observation with a planned caesarean at her local unit
options.rationale: Prolonged admission does not address the need for a surgical team and resources capable of managing massive haemorrhage. Where the birth happens matters more than how long she is observed beforehand. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta accreta spectrum)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging now and plan a caesarean hysterectomy at 34 weeks locally
options.rationale: Imaging may refine the assessment but committing to hysterectomy at this gestation and at a unit without the necessary support reverses the priorities. The location of birth is the decision that changes outcome. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta accreta spectrum)

explanation.summary: Placenta accreta spectrum describes abnormally adherent or invasive placentation, and its incidence has risen in step with caesarean section rates. The combination that should prompt suspicion is an anterior low lying placenta in a woman with previous uterine surgery, since the placenta implants over a scarred, poorly decidualised segment. Sonographic markers include loss of the retroplacental hypoechoic clear zone, irregular vascular lacunae, bladder wall interface irregularity and increased subplacental vascularity on Doppler. The single intervention that most reduces maternal morbidity is planned birth at around 34 to 36 weeks in a centre with a multidisciplinary team, massive transfusion capability and interventional radiology, since unanticipated accreta discovered at an emergency caesarean carries far higher rates of massive haemorrhage, intensive care admission and death.
key_points: Anterior low placenta plus previous caesarean is the classic risk combination
Loss of the clear zone and vascular lacunae suggest invasion rather than praevia
Invasion features do not resolve with advancing gestation
Planned birth in a tertiary centre is the main determinant of maternal outcome
Unanticipated accreta at emergency caesarean carries the worst outcomes
explanation.pearls: A woman with an anterior placenta praevia and two previous caesareans has a risk of placenta accreta spectrum of roughly forty per cent, which is why the finding prompts tertiary referral rather than a repeat scan.

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing a primary psychotic illness from a substance related one in a man with psychosis persisting a month after stopping methamphetamine
stem:
A 25 year old man is reviewed on your inpatient unit. He was admitted five weeks ago with persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations after heavy daily methamphetamine use over the preceding six months.

He has been in hospital throughout with supervised urine drug screens that have been negative for four weeks. He was started on olanzapine on admission and his agitation settled within days, but he continues to describe a belief that a neighbour is transmitting messages about him, and he still hears two voices commenting on his actions. His family mention that in the year before he started using, he had withdrawn from friends, stopped attending TAFE and spent most of his time alone in his room. He has no fever, no confusion and a normal neurological examination.

data_table.Examination: Persecutory delusion and third person auditory hallucinations persisting, no confusion, no fluctuation in conscious state, normal neurological examination
data_table.Investigations: Supervised urine drug screens negative for four weeks, full blood count electrolytes and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease the antipsychotic now, since his symptoms will resolve with continued abstinence alone
options.rationale: Symptoms that have already outlasted a month of abstinence are unlikely to be purely substance induced, and stopping treatment risks deterioration. Resolution within days to weeks is the expected pattern for a substance induced psychosis. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia clinical practice guideline)

options.text: Record a firm diagnosis of schizophrenia now and counsel him that treatment will be lifelong
options.rationale: Committing to a lifelong diagnosis at this point overstates the certainty available and can be difficult to revise once documented. The duration criterion and longitudinal course still need to be established. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia clinical practice guideline)

options.text: Switch to clozapine now, given that his symptoms have not resolved after five weeks of treatment
options.rationale: Treatment resistance requires failure of two adequate antipsychotic trials of sufficient dose and duration, and he has had only one. An adequate trial is generally considered to be at least four to six weeks at therapeutic dose. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia clinical practice guideline)

options.text: Continue the antipsychotic and reassess the diagnosis after a longer period of abstinence
options.rationale: Psychosis persisting more than a month beyond confirmed abstinence exceeds the expected course of a substance induced disorder and raises the likelihood of a primary psychotic illness, particularly given the premorbid decline his family describes. Continuing treatment while observing over time is the approach that avoids both premature labelling and undertreatment. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia clinical practice guideline)

options.text: Arrange lumbar puncture and autoimmune encephalitis antibody testing before altering treatment
options.rationale: Autoimmune encephalitis is suggested by confusion, seizures, movement disorder, autonomic instability or a fluctuating conscious state, none of which is present. His examination and course do not fit that pattern. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia clinical practice guideline)

explanation.summary: Separating a substance induced psychotic disorder from a primary psychotic illness that has been unmasked or accompanied by substance use is one of the harder judgements in general psychiatry, and it usually cannot be made at a single point in time. The most useful discriminator is the course of symptoms during confirmed abstinence, since a genuinely substance induced psychosis is expected to resolve within days to weeks once the drug is cleared. Features favouring a primary disorder include symptoms persisting well beyond that window, a premorbid decline in function preceding the substance use, prominent negative symptoms, and a family history of psychotic illness. A substantial proportion of people given an initial diagnosis of methamphetamine induced psychosis are later rediagnosed with schizophrenia, so the safest position early on is to treat the symptoms, verify abstinence objectively, and let the longitudinal course clarify the diagnosis rather than committing prematurely in either direction.
key_points: Substance induced psychosis is expected to resolve within days to weeks of abstinence
Persistence well beyond that window favours a primary psychotic illness
Premorbid functional decline before substance use is a key historical clue
Objectively verified abstinence is needed before the course can be interpreted
Many initial substance induced diagnoses are later revised to schizophrenia
explanation.pearls: Psychotic symptoms that persist beyond about one month of objectively verified abstinence from methamphetamine should shift the working diagnosis towards a primary psychotic illness, and the premorbid year is often where the answer already lies.

subtopic_detail: Neurological symptoms with a normal serum cobalamin and a raised methylmalonic acid in a man on long term metformin
stem:
A 64 year old man with type 2 diabetes attends your practice with six months of pins and needles in both feet that has progressed to his lower calves, and increasing unsteadiness when walking in the dark.

He has taken metformin 2 g daily for eleven years and his glycated haemoglobin has been consistently at target. On examination he has reduced vibration sense to the mid shin bilaterally, absent ankle reflexes with brisk knee reflexes, and a positive Romberg test. His full blood count shows a normal haemoglobin with a mean cell volume at the upper end of the range. His serum cobalamin is 165 pmol/L, his methylmalonic acid is raised and his homocysteine is raised. His thyroid function and folate are normal.

data_table.Examination: Reduced vibration sense to mid shin bilaterally, absent ankle reflexes with brisk knee reflexes, positive Romberg test, no visual field defect
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 138 g/L (130-180), mean cell volume 99 fL (80-100), serum cobalamin 165 pmol/L (150-700), methylmalonic acid raised, homocysteine raised, folate and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure him that the serum level is within range and review his symptoms again in six months
options.rationale: The serum assay measures total cobalamin including an inactive protein bound fraction and is insensitive at the lower end, which is exactly why the metabolite was measured. A normal range result does not exclude functional deficiency. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Attribute the symptoms to diabetic neuropathy and commence duloxetine for symptomatic relief
options.rationale: Diabetic neuropathy does not usually produce dorsal column signs with brisk knee reflexes, and his glycaemic control has been consistently good. Symptomatic treatment would leave a reversible cause untreated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Start parenteral cobalamin replacement now without waiting for further confirmatory testing
options.rationale: A raised methylmalonic acid demonstrates functional deficiency at tissue level even though the serum level sits within the reference range, and the combination of dorsal column and peripheral nerve signs indicates established neurological involvement. Delay risks irreversible cord damage, so replacement begins immediately. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Start oral folic acid replacement now and recheck his metabolites and blood count in three months
options.rationale: Folate given to a cobalamin deficient patient can correct the blood picture while the neurological damage continues to progress unchecked. His folate is in any case normal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the whole spine before starting any replacement therapy
options.rationale: Imaging may show dorsal column signal change but does not alter the decision to replace, and waiting for it delays treatment of an evolving cord lesion. The biochemistry has already established the diagnosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Cobalamin deficiency is frequently missed because the haematological and neurological manifestations do not track together, and neurological disease can be well advanced while the blood count remains entirely normal. The serum assay is an imperfect test because it measures total rather than metabolically available cobalamin, so patients with genuine tissue deficiency can return values within the reference range. Methylmalonic acid and homocysteine rise when the vitamin dependent reactions fail and therefore demonstrate functional deficiency, with methylmalonic acid the more specific of the two since homocysteine also rises in folate deficiency. Metformin impairs calcium dependent absorption of the cobalamin intrinsic factor complex in the terminal ileum and is a well recognised cause after several years of use, alongside pernicious anaemia, gastric surgery, ileal disease and dietary restriction. Subacute combined degeneration produces a characteristic mixture of dorsal column loss with upper motor neuron signs and a peripheral neuropathy, and neurological recovery depends heavily on how early replacement begins.
key_points: Neurological disease can precede any haematological abnormality
A serum level within range does not exclude functional deficiency
Methylmalonic acid is more specific than homocysteine for cobalamin deficiency
Long term metformin impairs ileal absorption of the vitamin
Neurological recovery depends on how early replacement is started
explanation.pearls: Absent ankle reflexes with brisk knee reflexes is the signature of subacute combined degeneration, where a peripheral neuropathy and a corticospinal tract lesion coexist in the same patient.

subtopic_detail: Spiral tibial fracture in a newly walking toddler with a witnessed low fall and no other injuries
stem:
A 16 month old boy is brought to your emergency department after his father saw him trip on the edge of a rug while running and twist as he fell onto carpet. He has refused to bear weight on the right leg since.

He began walking independently at 12 months. He is consoled easily and his father's account has been consistent each time it has been taken. On examination there is mild swelling over the lower right shin with tenderness, no bruising anywhere on his body, and full painless movement at the knee, hip and ankle. His skin, frenulum, ears and scalp are normal, and his growth and development are age appropriate. The radiograph shows an undisplaced spiral fracture of the distal tibial shaft with an intact fibula.

data_table.Examination: Mild swelling and tenderness over the distal right tibia, no bruising or other skin injury, normal frenulum ears and scalp, full painless movement of knee hip and ankle
data_table.Imaging: Undisplaced spiral fracture of the distal right tibial shaft with an intact fibula

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Above knee cast with a child protection notification made before the child leaves
options.rationale: Notification is driven by a mismatch between injury and explanation rather than by fracture type alone, and no such mismatch exists here. A spiral configuration is not by itself an indicator of inflicted injury in a mobile child. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Admit for a skeletal survey and ophthalmology review before any definitive fracture treatment
options.rationale: A skeletal survey is indicated for children under two when the injury is unexplained or inconsistent, which is not the case with this witnessed and congruent account. It would be correct had he been pre-mobile. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Above knee cast with routine fracture clinic review, without a child protection notification
options.rationale: A spiral fracture of the distal tibia in an independently walking toddler is a recognised accidental pattern produced by rotation on a planted foot, and the mechanism, mobility and consistent history fit it. There are no other injuries and no features that would make the account implausible. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Below knee backslab with fracture clinic review and blood tests for bone fragility
options.rationale: Metabolic bone investigation is prompted by multiple fractures, blue sclerae, wormian bones or a family history, none of which is present. A below knee cast also fails to control rotation at this level. (Source: RCH CPG: Fractures of the tibia and fibula)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Fractures of the tibia and fibula

options.text: Simple analgesia with weight bearing as tolerated and general practitioner review in one week
options.rationale: This fracture needs immobilisation to control rotational forces and to provide pain relief, so symptomatic management alone is inadequate. It would suit an undisplaced buckle fracture of the distal radius. (Source: RCH CPG: Fractures of the tibia and fibula)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Fractures of the tibia and fibula

explanation.summary: Deciding whether a fracture is accidental rests on whether the injury, the explanation, and the child's developmental stage are congruent, not on the fracture configuration alone. The spiral tibial fracture of early walking, sometimes described as a toddler's fracture, is produced by a twisting force through a planted foot and is a common accidental injury once a child is independently mobile. The features that should raise concern are a fracture in a child who is not yet mobile, an absent or changing explanation, delayed presentation, injuries of differing ages, or associated bruising in sites that do not take the impact of ordinary falls. Every child under two with a suspicious fracture warrants a skeletal survey, and inflicted injury should be considered alongside metabolic bone disease rather than instead of it.
key_points: Congruence of injury, explanation and developmental stage drives the assessment
Spiral tibial fractures are a recognised accidental pattern in walking toddlers
A fracture in a pre-mobile infant is the strongest single red flag
Skeletal survey is indicated under two years when the account is inconsistent
Metabolic bone disease is considered alongside, not instead of, inflicted injury
explanation.pearls: The developmental question that reframes a toddler fracture is whether the child walks independently: the same spiral tibial fracture that is unremarkable at sixteen months demands a skeletal survey in a six month old who cannot yet cruise.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Fractures of the tibia and fibula

subtopic_detail: Loss of the presenting part and a foetal bradycardia during labour in a woman with one previous caesarean
stem:
You are called to review a 32 year old woman at 39 weeks labouring spontaneously after one previous caesarean section for failure to progress. She has been progressing well and was 7 cm dilated with the head at the level of the spines thirty minutes ago.

Her epidural has been working well, but over the last few minutes she has become distressed by constant lower abdominal pain that persists between contractions, which is new. The cardiotocograph now shows a prolonged deceleration to 70/min lasting four minutes with no recovery. On vaginal examination the presenting part is now high and difficult to reach. Her contractions, which had been regular, have become infrequent and weak, and there is light fresh vaginal bleeding.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 126/min, blood pressure 96/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9 °C, foetal heart rate 70/min
data_table.Examination: Constant lower abdominal pain between contractions, presenting part high and difficult to reach, light fresh vaginal bleeding, contractions infrequent and weak
data_table.Monitoring: Prolonged deceleration to 70/min for four minutes with no recovery

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Give a subcutaneous tocolytic and reassess the foetal heart rate over the next ten minutes
options.rationale: Acute tocolysis is used for foetal distress from uterine hyperstimulation, where contractions are excessive rather than fading. It would delay definitive treatment of a mechanical catastrophe. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrapartum foetal surveillance)

options.text: Perform an amniotomy and apply a foetal scalp electrode to improve the quality of the trace
options.rationale: Improving trace quality addresses monitoring rather than the underlying event, and the presenting part is now too high to attach an electrode safely. The clinical picture already establishes urgency. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrapartum foetal surveillance)

options.text: Reposition her into the left lateral position and give a fluid bolus with high flow oxygen
options.rationale: Intrauterine resuscitation measures are appropriate for a deceleration from cord compression or hypotension, neither of which explains the loss of station and constant pain. They should not delay transfer to theatre here. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrapartum foetal surveillance)

options.text: Commence an oxytocin infusion to restore contractions and reassess progress in thirty minutes
options.rationale: Augmenting a uterus that may have ruptured risks extending the defect and causing catastrophic haemorrhage. Weakening contractions here reflect loss of uterine integrity rather than inadequate labour. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

options.text: Call the theatre team for immediate laparotomy with the neonatal and anaesthetic teams
options.rationale: Loss of station with constant pain, a deteriorating foetal heart rate and altered contractions in a scarred uterus indicates scar rupture, and both mother and baby are salvaged only by immediate operative delivery. Delay to confirm the diagnosis worsens outcomes for both. (Source: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section

explanation.summary: Vaginal birth after caesarean section is offered to suitable women in Australian practice, with uterine scar rupture the principal risk at roughly one in two hundred labours. Because rupture is uncommon, its recognition depends on assembling several individually unremarkable findings rather than on any single sign. An abnormal cardiotocograph is the commonest and earliest feature, and it is often accompanied by constant abdominal pain between contractions, cessation or weakening of previously effective contractions, loss of station of the presenting part, vaginal bleeding, haematuria, and maternal tachycardia with hypotension. Scar pain alone is a poor discriminator, particularly with an epidural in place. Management is immediate laparotomy, and the interval from diagnosis to delivery is the strongest determinant of neonatal outcome, so no investigation should precede transfer to theatre.
key_points: Scar rupture complicates roughly one in two hundred labours after caesarean
An abnormal cardiotocograph is the commonest and earliest sign
Loss of station and fading contractions indicate loss of uterine integrity
Epidural analgesia masks scar pain and reduces its diagnostic value
Time from diagnosis to delivery determines neonatal outcome
explanation.pearls: Weakening contractions in a woman labouring with a uterine scar is an ominous rather than a reassuring change, and augmenting with oxytocin at that moment can extend an existing rupture.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Birth after previous caesarean section
